name: Liam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the wheel loader crew at East Spur, a large limestone mine. I load broken stone into the crusher, inspect the tyres and bucket pins, and walk the new operators through the blind corners. I've got a two-year technical diploma and know that machine by sound. The dust gets into everything, and the split shifts leave me worn down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job mean at home now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and had hoped to work until about 66. My wife Celia and I have grown children, but we still help our son with rent some months. The mine pays me less than other leads because I took the shorter shift contract when my knee got bad. We have less than a month of bills saved, and there are few similar jobs near us. I have never used an AI tool; even the new roster app feels like more trouble than a printed sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the paperwork machine can have the paperwork. I still want a person walking around each loader before a shift. I would not spend lunch arguing about AI when we have a cracked mirror to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work may stay much the same, but our bank balance is already too low. I cannot miss many shifts with this knee, and Celia's pay from the laundry only covers part of our bills. A plateau would let me keep earning, yet it would not fill the savings account for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the loader shifts and hand the cracked mirror report to maintenance tomorrow. I'd transfer thirty from each pay packet into a separate bill reserve and ask our son if he can cover his next rent payment himself. In the first year I'd keep using paper checks until a new system proves accurate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job feels steady in this picture, but one knee flare could put the bills behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How often has your knee cost you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I missed three shifts last winter and the lost pay took two months to replace. I still do the job well when I am there. The numbers are just tighter than I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown son Mateo that we can help with groceries, but not his next rent bill. He might be upset. I would rather tell my grown son Mateo now than make a promise the bank cannot keep.

say: I would keep **human checks** on the loaders while letting software handle routine forms.
I would tell the crew the **cracked mirror** deserves attention before another app.
think: The job seems **steady**, but missing shifts could still upset our thin household budget.
Celia’s **laundry pay** covers only part of our bills, so a quiet AI path is no cure.
do: Keep the **loader shifts** and report the cracked mirror to maintenance tomorrow.
Transfer **thirty per payday** into a separate bill reserve and stop paying Mateo’s rent next month.
feel: **Uneasy** about ordinary bills despite stable work.
S0.quote: I would rather tell my grown son Mateo now than make a promise the bank cannot keep.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** and knee make routine lost shifts consequential even with no radical AI change.
The **rent conversation** is a concrete household cut that he dislikes but can carry out.

steps.text: Keep leading East Spur loader shifts and report the cracked mirror
Transfer thirty from each pay packet into a bill reserve
Stop covering Mateo’s next rent payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and ordering will change before our loader cabs do. I would want management to show the crew any proposed machine trial, with the safety checks attached. New machines should earn trust on a real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roster office might be smaller first, and later the mine might want fewer operators. I could lose my lead hours before I reach 66, and there are few other places here that need my skill. A short contract and weak savings make waiting expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current shifts and ask the foreman for the next twelve months of equipment plans in writing. I'd stop buying takeaway after night shifts and put forty more into the bill reserve each pay day. If a loader trial is ordered, I'd ask the crew representative about my contract terms before deciding on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The change is slower, but a single lost shift each week would hurt our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the trial is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A signed order and a date for the loader to come through the gate would do it. Slides in the lunch room would not. I have seen too many ideas disappear by the next budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about your contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a cut in lead shifts brings any notice or extra pay. I cannot plan around words from a manager in a corridor. I would take my contract to the representative.

say: I would ask for **written equipment plans** and proper safety checks before a loader trial.
I would say **office tasks** change before the heavy machines do.
think: Even a small **hours cut** could upset our bills before I reach my planned stopping age.
Few **local openings** make my experience less useful as a fallback.
do: Request **written plans** from the foreman and review contract terms if a trial is ordered.
Cut **night takeaway** and add forty each pay day to our bill reserve.
feel: **Anxious** because my own hours could shrink, with some time to respond.
S1.quote: A short contract and weak savings make waiting expensive.
fieldNote: He waits for a **signed order** before treating a machine trial as certain.
His **additional savings** come from a named recurring cut, not a vague promise to be careful.

steps.text: Request twelve months of written equipment plans from the foreman
Stop buying takeaway after night shifts
Add forty from each pay packet to the bill reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could take the planning sheets quickly, but the card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031. I would tell the crew to get the equipment schedule in writing. I do not want a lecture about opportunity while the roster is shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 in 2028 and 63 around the robot date, still three years short of when I hoped to stop. The office part of leading may go early; the loader seat could go later. With less than a month saved and few local jobs, losing that wage would put us in immediate trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Celia tonight to list every bill and stop helping Mateo with rent. This month I'd sell my spare motorbike if we can get a fair price, then put the proceeds into a bill reserve. In the first year after 2028 I'd ask the mine for an actual paid post on the remaining manual loaders and seek local income support if my hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I have a list of cuts, but it does not replace a wage for three years. I cannot see a reliable way across that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep paying first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing payment, food and Celia's travel to the laundry come before everything else. I would call the lender before missing a payment. I have never liked asking for help, but I would make that call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training for the remote loaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine offers a paid place tied to a real post, I would consider it, though screens are hard for me. I would not spend our last cash on a certificate without that promise. I would first ask what job is actually open.

say: I would mark **2028 paperwork** changes and the separate 2031 risk to loader seats.
I would seek a **written roster** and a real paid post on any remaining manual machines.
think: A lost **loader wage** around 2031 could leave us three years short of my planned retirement.
Our **tiny reserve** and few nearby jobs give me no reliable bridge.
do: Stop **rent help** for Mateo and sell the spare motorbike if the price is fair.
Ask for a **manual loader post** after 2028 and seek income support if hours fall.
feel: **Panicked** about a wage gap I cannot cover.
S2.quote: I have a list of cuts, but it does not replace a wage for three years.
fieldNote: He knows **2028 planning** changes precede the physical robot risk around 2031.
The **motorbike sale** would buy a little time, subject to a fair price.
He would consider **paid training** only for a real vacancy, without claiming one exists.

steps.text: Stop paying Mateo’s rent starting this month
Apply for local income support if loader hours fall
Ask for an open manual loader post after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that five years is enough time to count our shifts and demand a straight plan. Planning work could change in 2031; capable hands-on robots follow around 2034. I would ask for a written offer to older workers if the loader fleet changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the thinking system comes and 66 at the robot date. If the loader work lasts that long, I can stop close to the age I planned. The danger is the office part of my lead job disappearing earlier, or the mine cutting hours before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the first forty from each pay into our bill reserve starting now, and keep driving the loader. I'd ask the mine this year whether my lead contract can become a regular driving contract if planning duties go. In the first year after 2031 I'd take that role if offered and if the pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a path to 66, but the path depends on a contract the mine has not offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pay would be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Celia and I would add up housing, food and medicine first. A regular loader post needs to cover that monthly total after tax. I would not claim I can live on a number I have not calculated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a software course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would learn a new machine control if a supervisor showed it on shift, but I am not signing up for a screen course. I would put my energy into keeping the loader seat until 66.

say: I would ask for a **written driving offer** if planning duties leave my lead post.
I would separate **2031 desk work** from 2034 hands-on robot risk.
think: The **2034 robot date** reaches me near 66 if I keep enough driving shifts.
An earlier **hours cut** could still break the household budget.
do: Transfer **forty per payday** into a bill reserve starting now.
Ask for a **regular loader contract** and accept it after 2031 only if pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** because the plausible bridge rests on an unoffered contract.
S3.quote: I can see a path to 66, but the path depends on a contract the mine has not offered.
fieldNote: The **age calculation** gives him a possible working bridge to 66, subject to hours and pay.
He rejects **screen study** while remaining willing to learn controls on a paid shift.

steps.text: Transfer forty from each pay packet into a bill reserve
Keep operating the East Spur loader through the planning change
Take a regular driving role after 2031 if offered at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to plan if managers tell the crew the truth. AGI by 2036 could take the planning sheets, and capable hands-on robots arrive around 2039. I would ask for a yearly written fleet schedule, not another glossy presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the thinking date and 71 at the robot date. If I can work to 66, those changes would come after I stop. But our savings are so low that illness or a lost shift before then could still force me to leave early without enough money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job while my knee allows and save fifty more from each pay packet. This year Celia and I would ask the pension office for a written estimate at 66 and make a budget from it. In the first year after 2036, if I am retired, I would review the pension payments rather than assume they cover everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The technology dates give me room, but the next few years of ordinary bills still look narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change if the pension estimate is low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the housing costs first with Celia and ask about a cheaper place near our daughter. We would not move on a guess. I would want pension and housing costs on paper before moving to a cheaper home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise younger operators differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger operators to learn the remote controls if the mine pays them to practise. They have longer careers in front of them. My priority is keeping this knee and this wage working to 66.

say: I would seek a **yearly fleet schedule** while keeping the 2036 and 2039 changes separate.
I would tell younger operators to try **paid controls practice** while they have longer careers ahead.
think: The **AGI dates** may come after I stop, if I can work to 66.
Our **thin savings** still make illness or lost shifts a threat before retirement.
do: Keep the **loader job** while my knee allows and add fifty to savings each payday.
Get a **written pension estimate** this year and review actual payments after 2036 if retired.
feel: **Uneasy** about current bills and health, even with the technology dates later.
S4.quote: I would want pension and housing costs on paper before moving to a cheaper home.
fieldNote: The **ten-year timeline** protects his planned work horizon only if his health and shifts hold.
His **pension inquiry** is for planning; no retirement amount or entitlement is assumed.

steps.text: Keep operating the East Spur loader while the knee allows
Add fifty from each pay packet to family savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I could lose the office part of the lead job at 60 and the loader wage around 63, with almost nothing set aside. A paid place on a manual machine, honest notice and enough income support to cover a gap would help if those things actually materialised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask about bad knees and bad bank balances together. I can still teach a new loader driver how to hear a loose pin, but I cannot miss three shifts again. That is what keeps me watching the roster.

headlineQuote: I can still teach a new loader driver how to hear a loose pin, but I cannot miss three shifts again.
portrait: **Liam Reyes**, 58, leads wheel loader operators at a large limestone mine and is skilled at equipment and route checks.
A **shorter contract** leaves him on lower pay, with a sore knee, under one month saved and few nearby jobs.
He **avoids AI tools**, trusts printed records and wants to work until about 66 before stopping.
Fast AGI leaves him **panicked** over a three-year wage gap; slower dates help only if shifts and health hold.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could threaten lead duties at 60 and the loader wage near 63, before his planned stop at 66.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid manual post**, honest notice and income support for any uncovered wage gap would help if available.
